Central Europe. A cultural and geographic region stretching from Western Europe to the Soviet Union, historically centered on the Danube basin and the Austro-Hungarian Empire. Its peoples—Poles, Czechs, Hungarians, Slovaks, Romanians—speak Indo-European languages and practice Christianity predominantly. The region has been perpetually contested, claimed by empires from both west and east, and carved up by the world wars, the Cold War, and post-Cold War reconfiguration.

Geographically, Central Europe is bounded by the Alps to the west and the Carpathian Mountains to the east. The Danube River flows through its heart, historically linking it economically to the Balkans and the Black Sea. The Austro-Hungarian Empire from eighteen sixty-seven to nineteen eighteen was the dominant regional power, uniting Czechs, Hungarians, Poles, Romanians, and South Slavs under a dual monarchy. When it collapsed after the First World War, it created the modern nation-states we know today.

After the Second World War, the region was divided. Western zones became independent or neutral, while Soviet-controlled zones became satellite states until nineteen eighty-nine through nineteen ninety-one. The Prague Spring in nineteen sixty-eight symbolized the region's desire for autonomy, but Soviet tanks crushed it, reinforcing Soviet dominance and the Cold War divide.

Since nineteen eighty-nine, Central European nations—Poland, the Czech Republic, Hungary, and Slovakia—have joined NATO and the European Union, reorienting westward and integrating into Western institutions. The region is culturally and linguistically distinct from both Western Europe, with its Romance and Germanic languages, and from Eastern Europe and Russia with their Slavic speech. This "in-between" status has shaped its historical trajectory. Today, Central Europe is relatively prosperous and stable compared to its neighbors, though nationalist movements and illiberal governance have emerged in recent years. Its history connects it to Eastern Europe, which shared Soviet domination, to the Danube River as its defining geographic and economic feature, to the Austro-Hungarian Empire as its dominant historical power, to the Cold War that shaped it for forty-five years, to the Prague Spring as the iconic resistance to Soviet dominance, and to the Holy Roman Empire as its early medieval predecessor.
